meta.blurb: Born a slave in Virginia, Booker Washington walked and begged his way to school, swept a classroom to prove himself, and later built a famous college from nothing. Here is his own honest, hopeful story of work, learning and courage.
meta.bible: Booker Washington: born enslaved on a small farm near Hale's Ford, Franklin County, Virginia, about 1856; the founder of Tuskegee; died on 14 November 1915. Jane: his mother, the cook on the farm. John: his older brother. Washington Ferguson: his stepfather, who worked in the salt furnaces of Malden. Viola Ruffner: the strict Vermont-born woman of Malden who taught him thoroughness. Mary Mackie: the Hampton teacher who tested him with a room to sweep. General Samuel Armstrong: the founder of Hampton Institute and Booker's inspiration. Hampton Institute: the school in Virginia where Booker studied and taught. Malden: the West Virginia town of the salt furnaces. Tuskegee: the town in Alabama where Booker opened his school on 4 July 1881. Olivia Davidson: a gifted teacher who helped build Tuskegee. General Marshall: the Hampton treasurer who lent five hundred dollars. Porter Hall: the first big brick building. Aunt Caroline Smith: the old woman who gave six eggs. George Washington Carver: the scientist who joined Tuskegee in 1896. Grover Cleveland: the President who praised the Atlanta speech. William McKinley: the President who visited Tuskegee in 1898. Theodore Roosevelt: the President who invited Booker to dinner in 1901. William Du Bois: a critic of Booker's views. Atlanta Exposition: the fair of September 1895 where Booker gave his famous speech. National Negro Business League: the group he founded in 1900. Harvard: the university that gave him an honorary degree in 1896. Virginia. West Virginia. Alabama. Richmond. Boston. Atlanta. Vermont. Cotton States. Negro Conference: the farmers' meeting begun in 1892. Up From Slavery: the title of the book, published in 1901. Union. Native American. Webster. Booker Taliaferro Washington: his full name. Voice and tone: honest, humble and warm, with quiet humour; facts stated plainly and without gore; the book is a hopeful life story, and where historians disagree about his ideas or the dates the retelling says so.

B1B2: Booker Washington was born a slave on a small farm in Virginia, most likely in 1856. He never knew his exact birthday, and he knew nothing about his white father.
Booker lived with his mother, Jane, in a cabin that was also the farm's kitchen. It had a dirt floor, no glass in the windows, and a hole in the ground where sweet potatoes were kept.
Booker's only piece of clothing as a small boy was a shirt made of rough flax. It felt like a hundred needles on his skin, until his kind older brother John wore it for a while to make it softer.
Booker had to carry his young mistress's books to the schoolhouse each day. Through the door he saw many children studying, and he felt that to go inside would be like entering paradise.

One morning in 1865, a stranger stood in front of the house and read a paper to everyone on the farm. It said that they were free, and the slaves sang and cheered, though some also began to wonder what they would do next.

After freedom, Booker's family travelled to Malden, in West Virginia, where his stepfather, Washington Ferguson, had found work. They walked and rode in a wagon for many days, and Booker was about nine years old.
In Malden, Booker worked in a salt furnace, starting at four o'clock in the morning. He learned to read the number eighteen from the barrels he had to mark.

Booker's mother somehow found a spelling book for him, and he taught himself the alphabet. Soon a young Black teacher arrived in Malden, but Booker had to work in the furnace before school and could only go at night.

At school the teacher called the names, and Booker realised that he had only one name. He quickly gave his name as Booker Washington, and later he learned that his mother had also called him Booker Taliaferro.

When Booker worked in a coal mine, he overheard two miners talking about a school called Hampton Institute. It was far away, but students there could work to pay for their lessons, and he decided to go.
Booker became a houseboy for Mrs Viola Ruffner, a strict woman from New England. She taught him to do every job completely and cleanly, and she also let him read in her library.
When he was about sixteen, Booker set off for Hampton, which was about five hundred miles away. His mother and his brother John said goodbye, and neighbours gave him small gifts of money.
Booker reached Richmond at night, with no money and nowhere to stay. He slept under a raised sidewalk, and next day he unloaded a ship to earn food and money for the last miles.
Booker arrived at Hampton with only fifty cents in his pocket. The head teacher, Miss Mary Mackie, told him to sweep a classroom, so he swept it three times, and she could find no dirt.

To pay for his room and food, Booker became the school janitor, getting up early to light fires and clean. He met General Samuel Armstrong, who had founded Hampton, and felt that he was the greatest man he had ever known.
At Hampton, students learned to take baths, brush their teeth, keep their rooms tidy and behave politely. They also learned a trade, and Booker came to believe that useful work has real dignity.
Booker worked hard and finished his studies at Hampton in 1875. He went back to Malden, where the whole town welcomed him as a teacher.
Booker taught a day school for children and a night school for adults who worked all day. He was surprised and moved by the older people who came, often tired, to learn to read.
General Armstrong invited Booker to come back to Hampton as a teacher. There Booker looked after a group of Native American students and also ran a night school for older students.
In 1881, a letter came from Alabama asking General Armstrong to recommend a white man to start a new school for Black students. Armstrong wrote back that he knew just the person, and it was Booker.
When Booker reached Tuskegee in June 1881, he found that there was no land, no building and no equipment. The state gave only two thousand dollars a year for teachers, and nothing for anything else.
Booker spent a month riding through the countryside to meet local families. He found people living in one-room cabins, eating fat pork and cornbread, with children who could not go to school.
The school opened on 4 July 1881 in a run-down building beside a church, with about thirty students. Many of them were adults who had already worked as teachers and wanted to learn more.
At Tuskegee, Booker insisted that students keep their rooms tidy, wash daily and brush their teeth. He called the toothbrush a sign of civilisation, and he did not mind teaching such small things.
Olivia Davidson, a gifted teacher, joined Tuskegee and became one of Booker's most important helpers. She travelled to the North to ask for gifts of money, and Booker later married her.
The school soon needed more room, and an old, run-down plantation of about a hundred acres was for sale. Booker borrowed five hundred dollars from the treasurer of Hampton to make the first payment.
Students cleared brush and trees from the old farm with axes and spades. They planted crops, and in this way they learned about farming while they also fed the school.
The students wanted to make their own bricks, but the first kilns failed, and they had no money to try again. Booker pawned his watch for fifteen dollars, and the next kiln produced good bricks.
Using their own bricks, the students built a large new building named Porter Hall. As they worked, they learned bricklaying, carpentry and painting, skills that would help them earn a living.
Tuskegee combined classroom lessons with practical work in farming, carpentry, cooking and sewing. Booker believed that people who could do useful work well would always be respected.
Booker was sometimes insulted on trains and in hotels because he was Black. He decided not to let it make him bitter, because he felt that hatred would harm him more than the people who insulted him.
One day an elderly woman named Aunt Caroline Smith came to the school with six eggs as a gift. She had very little, but she wanted to help the students, and the gift touched Booker deeply.
To keep the school open, Booker travelled to the North and spoke to wealthy people. He did not beg; instead, he described the school's work simply and let the results speak for themselves.
In 1892, Booker invited farmers and workers to Tuskegee for a yearly meeting called the Negro Conference. They shared advice about growing better crops, saving money, avoiding debt and buying land.

In 1896, a gifted scientist named George Washington Carver came to teach at Tuskegee. He studied plants and soil, and he later became famous for showing farmers how to grow crops like peanuts and sweet potatoes.
General Armstrong died in 1893, and Booker felt a deep sense of loss. He had learned from him that great work needs both patience and generosity, and he promised to carry on his work.

In September 1895, Booker received an invitation to speak at the Cotton States Exposition in Atlanta. He knew that thousands of people, both Black and white, would listen, so he prepared very carefully.

In his speech, Booker told a story about a ship lost at sea, whose crew were dying of thirst. A passing ship said to them, Cast down your bucket where you are, and when they did, they found that the water was fresh.
Booker held up his hand and said that in social matters the races could remain as separate as the fingers. Yet, he added, in all things that matter for progress, they could be as one, like a hand.

When Booker finished, the audience stood up and cheered, and newspapers across the country printed his speech. President Grover Cleveland wrote him a warm letter, and he became a famous man overnight.

Some Black leaders, including William Du Bois, said that the speech gave up too much on voting rights and equal treatment. Booker's supporters answered that he was doing what was possible in a dangerous time.
In 1896 Harvard University gave Booker an honorary master's degree. He was the first Black man to receive an honorary degree from Harvard, and he wrote that he was greatly surprised.
In December 1898 President William McKinley came to Tuskegee with members of his government. They toured the buildings and the farm, and the President praised the school, which pleased Booker.

In less than twenty years, Tuskegee grew from thirty students in an old shack into a school with hundreds of students and many buildings. Most of these buildings were built by the students themselves.
Booker often said that no people could succeed until they learned that farming a field is as dignified as writing a poem. He wanted Black Americans to build skills, savings and property.
In 1900, Booker founded the National Negro Business League in Boston. Its aim was to help Black people open businesses, share ideas and support one another.
Booker told his life story in a series of magazine articles in 1900 and 1901. They were then published as a book called Up From Slavery, which sold widely and was translated into many languages.

In October 1901, President Theodore Roosevelt invited Booker to dinner at the White House, the first time a Black guest had been invited in this way. Many white Southerners were angry, but Booker's reputation grew.
Booker Washington died at Tuskegee on 14 November 1915, when he was about fifty-nine. He had worked hard to the end, and thousands of people came to honour him.
Tuskegee is now a university, and part of its campus is a national historic site where visitors can learn about Booker's life. His book is still read, and people still argue about his ideas.
C1C2: Booker Taliaferro Washington was born into slavery on a small farm in Franklin County, Virginia, most probably in 1856, though he himself believed it was a year or two later. Like most children of the enslaved he never learned his exact birthday, and of his white father he knew nothing at all. In the book that he wrote as an old man he begins his story with these uncertain, humble facts.

Booker's home was a crude cabin that also served as the kitchen of the plantation, where his mother, Jane, cooked for the white family. It had a dirt floor, a cat hole to let the cat in and out, and a pit in one corner where sweet potatoes were stored for the winter. Each night the children slept on a heap of rags, and in the cold the draughts blew through the cracks in the walls.

As a small boy Booker owned just one garment, a long shirt of rough flax that was said to feel like a hundred pin-points scratching his skin. It was his older brother John who rescued him, for he would wear the new shirt until it had been softened, taking the pain upon himself. Booker never forgot this small act of love, and he mentions it many years later.

Each morning Booker was required to carry the books of his young mistress to the little schoolhouse, and he lingered at the door to look at the children inside. The sight of so many boys and girls bent over their lessons filled him with a longing that he could hardly describe, and he thought that to be allowed to go in would be like entering paradise. It was a wish that he held onto, quietly and stubbornly, through many hard years of work.

In the spring of 1865 the enslaved people of the farm were called to the front of the house, where a stranger read aloud a paper that proclaimed them free. There was singing, laughter and prayer, and Booker's mother, who bent over him, seemed to him to be crying with joy. By the next day, however, a quiet seriousness had settled over the cabins, for freedom brought the great question of how each family was to live.

After emancipation, Booker's mother took her children to Malden, West Virginia, where her husband, Washington Ferguson, had found work at the salt furnaces. The journey of some two hundred miles was made in a wagon and on foot, and it took the little family many days of slow travel. At the end of the road he found a rough town, crowded and noisy, but it was also a place where he could go to school.

In Malden the boy was put to work packing salt, beginning at four in the morning, long before the sun rose and long before school began. He learned the number eighteen by copying it from the barrels that bore the number of the furnace, and he took such pride in this small achievement that he practised making the figures until he could do so without effort. It was his first real lesson in reading, and, strangely enough, it came from a salt barrel.

Booker's mother, though she could not read herself, somehow obtained a copy of Webster's spelling book, and the boy began to teach himself the alphabet, a letter at a time. When a young Black teacher arrived in Malden, the family could not afford to lose Booker's wages, so for a long time he attended only a night school after his long hours at the furnace. Even when he was tired and hungry, he went to the night class every evening of the week.

On his first day in school, Booker realised that other children had two names while he had only one, so when the teacher called for his full name he promptly replied that it was Booker Washington. He later discovered that his mother had given him the middle name Taliaferro at birth, and so he added it back, becoming Booker Taliaferro Washington. Freedom, he reflects, gave people the chance to choose who they would be, even in something as small as a name.

Later, while working in a coal mine, Booker overheard two miners speaking of a great school for Black students called Hampton Institute, hundreds of miles away in Virginia. They said that poor young men and women could work for their board there and so receive an education, and the boy promptly resolved that he would go, no matter how far. The thought of Hampton became the guiding star of his life, and he never let it fade.

Booker found work as a houseboy in the home of Mrs Viola Ruffner, a stern but fair woman from Vermont, who had the reputation of being impossible to please. Under her sharp eye he learned to do every task thoroughly, from sweeping a floor to weeding a garden, and she also encouraged his reading and let him study at odd hours. Years later he would say that he owed her more than he could express.

At about the age of sixteen, Booker set out for Hampton, which lay some five hundred miles from Malden, carrying a small bag and a few coins collected from friends and neighbours. His mother, gave him her blessing, though she had little else to give, and watched him go with pride. His brother John, who had saved some money, helped to pay for the first stage of the journey.

After many days on stagecoaches and slow trains, Booker arrived in Richmond, Virginia, at night, tired, hungry and without a cent in his pocket. Unable to afford a bed, he crept under a raised wooden sidewalk and slept there, hearing the footsteps of passers-by above his head, and in the morning he found work unloading a ship. The wages bought him breakfast and a little extra, and he gratefully resumed his journey.

Booker reached Hampton at last with just fifty cents in his pocket, dirty, ragged and exhausted, and the teacher in charge, Miss Mary Mackie, hesitated to admit him. After some time she told him to sweep a classroom, and, remembering Mrs Ruffner, he swept it three times and dusted every piece of furniture four times, while she tested the corners with her handkerchief. Finding no dust, she said quietly that she thought he would do for the institution.

To pay for his board, Booker was made a janitor at Hampton, which meant rising before dawn to light fires and sweeping and dusting long after the other students had gone to bed. There he met General Samuel Chapman Armstrong, a former Union officer who had founded the school, and he felt, even from a distance, that he was in the presence of a truly great man. The janitor's work, he says, taught him as much as any lesson in a classroom, and he never forgot it.

At Hampton, Booker learned lessons that were not in any book: how to take a bath, clean his teeth, keep a room tidy and behave with courtesy toward others. Every student worked at a trade as well as studying, and the sight of young people proud of a well-made shoe or a clean floor taught him that useful labour has its own dignity. These ideas would stay with him for the rest of his life and shape everything he later built.

Working and studying for three years, Booker completed his course at Hampton and graduated in 1875, a former salt packer now holding a diploma. His return to Malden was greeted with delight by his family and friends, who came out to see the young man who had gone to school hundreds of miles away. Almost at once, he was asked to take charge of the town's school for Black children.

Back in Malden, Booker ran a day school for children and a night school for men and women who laboured all day in the furnaces and mines. Some of the pupils were old enough to be his grandparents, and many came after a twelve-hour shift, yet they sat down eagerly to learn their letters. Seeing their hunger for knowledge only deepened his faith in the power of education to change a life.

In 1879 General Armstrong invited Booker back to Hampton, where he was asked to take charge of a group of young Native American men who had been sent to the school from the western plains. He also organised a night school for working students, and he writes warmly of his Native American pupils, who, he says, taught him as much as he taught them. His growing skill as a teacher soon came to the notice of people far beyond the little town.

In 1881 a letter arrived at Hampton from a small town in Alabama called Tuskegee, asking General Armstrong to recommend a principal for a new school for Black students, and presuming that he would recommend a white man. Armstrong replied that he knew of only one suitable candidate, a Black graduate named Booker Washington, and after some anxious suspense the formal offer came. Washington was about twenty-five years old and had never before run a school of his own.

When Booker reached Tuskegee in June 1881, he discovered that the so-called school consisted of nothing at all: no land, no buildings, no equipment and not a single pupil. The Alabama legislature had promised two thousand dollars a year for teachers' salaries, but not a cent for property or supplies. Many a man would have turned around and gone home, but Booker saw only a blank page on which he might begin to write.

Before opening the school he spent a month travelling about the countryside in a borrowed cart, visiting the cabins of poor farmers and talking to them about their lives. He found large families crowded into a single room, eating cornbread and fatty pork from one dish, with no books and often no way for the children to attend school. The experience convinced him that his work must begin with the practical needs of ordinary people.

On 4 July 1881, the Tuskegee Normal School opened its doors in a shabby building beside a church, with about thirty pupils and one teacher, Booker Washington. Many of the students were older than their teacher, and several were already schoolteachers themselves, who came to improve their own education so that they could return and teach others. The first term was poor, cramped and uncomfortable, but it was a beginning, and everyone knew it.

Booker did not think any detail too small for a school, and he insisted that students keep their rooms tidy, bathe regularly, mend their clothes and use a toothbrush every day. The toothbrush, he declared half-seriously, was an important sign of civilisation, and he judged each student's progress by habits as much as by examination results. In his view a person who learned to take care of the little things would be ready for the great ones.

Soon a gifted teacher named Olivia Davidson joined the school, and Washington came to rely on her as an energetic partner whose courage and judgement he praised again and again. She travelled to the North to give concerts and speak to church groups, raising money for the school, and she later became his second wife. Without her work, he says, Tuskegee might not have survived its first hard years.

The cramped school soon needed more room, and when an abandoned plantation of some hundred acres came on the market, Washington determined to buy it, though he had no money. He borrowed five hundred dollars from the treasurer at Hampton, General Marshall, and made the first payment on land that had been worn out by years of cotton growing. The old farm lay on a low hill, not far from the town, and it would soon become the centre of the school.

On the new land the students themselves cleared away brambles, cut down trees and ploughed the exhausted fields, and in doing so they acquired a practical education in farming. Washington worked beside them, with a pair of old clothes and a spade, and showed that no one at Tuskegee was above manual work. The crops they planted helped to feed the school, and the work taught pride as well as skill.

Washington decided that the school should make its own bricks, but none of the students or teachers had ever built a kiln, and the first attempt collapsed in the middle of the burning. After a second failure, with no money left for another try, he pawned his watch for fifteen dollars to buy the necessary materials, and this time the kiln worked. The bricks were good, and, to everyone's delight, the school had suddenly acquired a new industry.

With bricks from their own kilns, the students now built their first large school building, Porter Hall, which they raised with their own hands, brick by brick and board by board. As they worked, they learned bricklaying, carpentry and painting, practical crafts that would later earn them a living and win the respect of their white neighbours. In time, nearly every building on the Tuskegee campus was built in this way.

Washington designed the course at Tuskegee so that every student combined classroom study with training in a practical skill, whether farming, carpentry, blacksmithing, cooking or sewing. He believed that people who could do useful work thoroughly would always find a place in society, and that their skills would, in time, win them the respect that no argument could. He did not scorn academic learning, but he insisted that it should be put to use.

In his travels Washington was sometimes refused a hotel room or a seat in a railway carriage because of his colour, and he describes these insults without self-pity. He resolved never to allow any man to narrow his soul by making him hate, for he believed that hatred poisons the person who feels it far more than the object of it. This calm refusal to be provoked became one of the chief sources of his influence.

One day an elderly woman named Aunt Caroline Smith, who had been born a slave and still lived in extreme poverty, came to the school and offered six eggs as her contribution to its work. Washington was deeply moved, for he understood that she was giving more, in proportion to her means, than any rich donor, and that she had done so out of faith in the students. He tells the story to illustrate the great hopes that ordinary people had pinned on Tuskegee.

To keep the school open, Washington spent many weeks each year travelling in the North, speaking in churches and parlours and calling on wealthy people who might support the work. He did not plead or press, but described what the students were doing in simple, honest language and let the results speak for themselves. Over the years, this patient method won him friends and donors, and gifts began to arrive from many quarters.

In 1892 Washington invited the farmers and labourers of the neighbourhood to a meeting at Tuskegee, which became known as the Negro Conference, and some four hundred of them crowded into the hall. They spoke frankly about debt, about the cost of rented land and about the crops that gave the best return, and they went home with practical ideas for living more independently. The conference became an annual event and spread to other parts of the South.

In 1896 the school welcomed a remarkable new teacher, George Washington Carver, a scientist who had studied agriculture and wanted to help poor Southern farmers. In his laboratory at Tuskegee he studied soils and plants, and he taught farmers how to rotate their crops and to grow peanuts and sweet potatoes, which restored the exhausted land. His patient research would make him one of the best-known American scientists of his time.

In 1893 General Armstrong, the founder of Hampton and Washington's chief inspiration, died after a long illness, and Booker travelled to Hampton to join the mourners. He had learned from the General that great work demands patience, generosity and an unselfish belief in the capacity of others, and he wrote of him with warmth and gratitude. He felt that the best way to honour his teacher was to carry his ideas further.

In September 1895 Washington was asked to speak at the opening of the Cotton States and International Exposition in Atlanta, an honour that no Black speaker had yet received there. He knew that thousands of people, Black and white, Northern and Southern, would be listening, and that anything he said might be repeated across the country, so he prepared with enormous care. On the platform, he says, his heart was beating so loudly that he could hardly hear himself.

Washington's speech told the story of a ship lost at sea whose sailors were dying of thirst until a passing vessel signalled them to cast down their bucket where they were. When they did so, they discovered that they were sailing in the fresh water of a great river's mouth, and their salvation had been beside them all along. He used the story to urge both races in the South to work together and to build on the opportunities already around them.

Holding up his hand with the fingers spread, Washington declared that in all things purely social, Black and white Southerners could be as separate as the fingers, yet as one hand in all things essential to mutual progress. The phrase went around the country, applauded by many as a promise of peace and attacked by others as an acceptance of segregation. It was a sentence that history would go on to debate for well over a century to come.

When Washington finished, the audience rose to its feet and cheered, many of them in tears, and within hours the telegraph had carried his words to newspapers across the nation. President Grover Cleveland wrote him a warm letter of congratulation, and in a single afternoon the head of a small Alabama school became a national figure. Invitations to speak and offers of money arrived in great numbers over the following weeks.

Not everyone admired the speech, and critics such as William Du Bois later argued that Washington had accepted second-class status for Black citizens and had said too little about the vote and about equal rights. His defenders replied that he was working in a dangerous time, when open protest could bring violence, and that he supported progress in quieter ways. Historians still disagree about which of the two views is nearer to the truth.

In 1896 Harvard University awarded Washington an honorary Master of Arts degree, and he was the first African American to receive an honorary degree from that university. He describes the day with characteristic modesty, remarking that he was astonished that a boy who had once swept a floor to enter school should now be honoured in such a famous place. The honour brought new respect for the work that was being done at Tuskegee.

In December 1898 President William McKinley, accompanied by several members of his cabinet, visited Tuskegee, where the students put on a demonstration of their work in the classrooms, workshops and fields. The visitors were impressed by the neatness, the discipline and the evident pride of the pupils, and they spoke warmly of the school's achievements. For Washington, it was the proof that the institution had won attention at the highest level.

In less than twenty years, Tuskegee grew from a single shabby building and thirty pupils into a flourishing school with hundreds of students, dozens of teachers and a campus of well-made brick buildings. Most of those buildings had been constructed by students, who had learned trades while serving the school, and graduates were now spreading across the South to teach what they had learned. Washington was justly proud of all this, but he took great care to share the credit with others.

Washington often repeated that no race can prosper until it learns that there is as much dignity in tilling a field as in writing a poem, and this idea lay at the centre of his philosophy. He believed that Black Americans who built skills, saved money and owned land would eventually win the respect of their neighbours, and that this practical strength would protect their rights. Critics thought this approach far too slow, but many ordinary people took it to heart.

In 1900 Washington founded the National Negro Business League, which held its first meeting in Boston and which brought together Black merchants, bankers, farmers and tradespeople from many states. Its aim was to encourage Black-owned enterprises, to share useful knowledge and to prove that economic independence was within reach. Local branches were soon established across the country, and the League continued to grow for years.

Washington wrote the story of his life in a series of magazine chapters during 1900 and 1901, and they were collected in a book called Up From Slavery, which quickly became a bestseller. It was translated into many languages and became the most widely read account of the life of a formerly enslaved person, apart from that of Frederick Douglass. Its simple, modest tone, and its message of hope, appealed to readers around the world.

In October 1901, a few months after the book appeared, President Theodore Roosevelt invited Washington to dine at the White House, the first time that an African American had been a guest of a President at a meal there. Many white Southern newspapers reacted with fury, but Black Americans, and many white Northerners, saw the invitation as a sign of respect. It showed how much influence he had gained since the day he first swept a classroom.

Booker Washington died at Tuskegee on 14 November 1915, at about the age of fifty-nine, worn out by decades of travelling, speaking and fund-raising. Thousands of students, teachers, graduates and townspeople attended the funeral, and he was buried on the campus beside the school that had been the work of his life. The little school that had begun with thirty pupils in a borrowed building had grown into one of the best-known institutions in America.

Today Tuskegee is a university, and part of its historic campus is a national park where visitors can walk among the buildings the first students built. Up From Slavery is still widely read and discussed, admired for its courage and humour and challenged for its cautious politics, and its author remains one of the most debated figures in American history. Whatever one decides, it is hard not to be moved by the journey of a boy who carried books to a schoolhouse door and eventually opened one of his own.
